title: Don’t Blame Phones for Teen Sadness
author: Dario Marino
content:
![Don’t Blame Phones for Teen
Sadness](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-16-at-8.21.19
---AM.png)

Young people are unhappy, and many observers think they know what is to blame:
technology. The most influential argument in this direction comes from the
psychologist Jonathan Haidt. In his 2024 book _The Anxious Generation_ , Haidt
argued that giving young people smartphones in the early 2010s "rewired"
childhood, which led to large upticks in anxiety, depression, and related
ailments. Haidt's argument has begun to influence policymakers in many
locales, informing efforts to limit phone use in schools and to restrict youth
access to social media platforms.

It is understandable why this story has proven attractive. The diffusion of
mobile internet technology was a big change, and it's easy to imagine that
being constantly connected makes us feel anxious, self-conscious, and
dissatisfied. However, there are problems with this account. For one thing,
what do we make of the fact that English-speaking countries are significantly
sadder than other countries where youth smartphone access is just as
widespread? If it were just the phone, wouldn't teens in other parts of the
world be just as unhappy? It would be one thing if Anglophone youth reported
greater use of digital technology than their counterparts elsewhere, but they
don't.

If you rank the six regions in the [_2026 World Happiness
Report_](https://www.worldhappiness.report/ed/2026/adolescent-life-
satisfaction-and-social-media-use-gender-differences-in-an-international-
dataset/?ref=compactmag.com) by how much time teenage girls spend on social
media, English-speaking countries aren't in first place. Latin America has a
larger share of heavy users, five or more hours a day, than the Anglosphere
does. But Latin American girls at the heaviest use levels report far less
unhappiness than English-speaking girls at the same use levels, and English-
speaking countries still post the steepest collapse and the highest ceiling of
low life satisfaction of any region. If dosage explained the outcome, the
region with the heaviest users should look the worst. Instead, the region with
more heavy users looks better, and the region with lighter use looks worse by
a wide margin. An almost identical social media usage pattern can be found in
Western Europe, but its users are happier at any level compared to teen social
media users in the English-speaking world. Likewise, in a [_cross-cultural
study_](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/10447318.2025.2480909?ref=compactmag.com)
comparing Britons and Arabs who spent the same amount of time on social media,
the Brits came out significantly less happy.
